summary: This informational memo covers security for provider-provisioned VPNs. It describes threats, including those from malicious behaviour inside or outside the network, and defensive techniques, and lists security requirements for such services.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4111 describes security risks and possible defenses for VPNs configured and managed by a service provider. It gives customers and providers a shared set of requirements and a template for evaluating a specific VPN technology.

subtitle: Threats, defenses, and evaluation questions for provider-provisioned virtual private networks.

tldr.problem: A provider-provisioned VPN shares network infrastructure, so customers and providers need to understand threats to traffic, equipment, and separation between VPNs.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a trusted-zone model, catalogs threats and defenses, describes user and provider security requirements, and supplies a template for evaluating specific technologies.
tldr.outcome: It is a framework and checklist rather than a protocol or a complete set of requirements for every VPN technology. It has been updated by RFC 8996.

today: RFC 4111 is Informational and has been updated by RFC 8996. It provides a PPVPN security framework and evaluation checklist, not a protocol.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
A Provider-Provisioned Virtual Private Network (PPVPN) is configured and managed by a service provider. RFC 4111 discusses threats to these services, defensive techniques, monitoring and reporting, possible user requirements, and provider responsibilities.

The RFC does not analyze individual PPVPN technologies or prescribe the exact mechanisms each technology must implement. It also leaves special security considerations caused by IP mobility outside its scope. Instead, it provides a common framework and a checklist for later technology-specific analysis.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC helps customers and providers discuss PPVPN security. It describes risks and ways to assess protection, but does not decide which mechanisms every implementation must use.

sections.title: The Trusted-Zone Model
sections.content:
The RFC treats each PPVPN as a trusted zone and the PPVPN core as another trusted zone. A Customer Edge (CE) device sits in the customer network; a Provider Edge (PE) device connects the provider network to a customer; and a Provider (P) router connects PE routers in the core.

The central security concern is a breach from outside a trusted zone to its inside. The VPN should remain secure even though its core infrastructure is shared with other VPNs. Attacks that begin inside the same zone as their target, and general network-security issues unrelated to PPVPNs, are outside the framework's scope.
sections.plainLanguage: The model separates each customer's VPN from the provider's core and from other VPNs. Sharing the core must not let traffic or control information cross into the wrong VPN.

sections.title: Threats to Traffic and Control Systems
sections.content:
Data-plane attacks target customer traffic. They include observing, changing, deleting, replaying, or inserting packets, analyzing traffic patterns, and denying service. Possible sources include other customers, provider staff, people with physical access to provider sites, social engineering, and attackers on the Internet.

Control-plane attacks target the systems that operate the service. Examples include denial of service against provider equipment, unauthorized management access, incorrect connections between VPNs, attacks on routing or address separation, and attacks on control protocols used for membership discovery or tunnel setup. The RFC notes that cross-connection between VPNs is a major concern for users.
sections.plainLanguage: An attacker may target the customer's packets or the systems that direct them. A serious control-plane error can send traffic to the wrong VPN, while a data-plane attack can expose, change, or disrupt traffic.

sections.title: Defensive Techniques
sections.content:
The RFC describes techniques rather than requirements for every PPVPN. Encryption can protect traffic on CE-to-PE links, between PEs, or between CEs, depending on which parts of the network the customer trusts. It can add processing work, configuration effort, and packet length, and can limit the provider's ability to inspect traffic for other services.

Other techniques include authenticating VPN members and control messages, filtering packets, using firewalls, separating infrastructure, limiting each VPN's resource use, and improving provider configuration processes. Monitoring should detect and report attacks through a protected channel. Reporting should be designed so that many events do not flood the network or monitoring system.
sections.plainLanguage: Providers can choose where to encrypt traffic and can also use authentication, filters, resource limits, and operational checks. The right choices depend on which parts of the network the customer trusts and what service is needed.

sections.title: User and Provider Requirements
sections.content:
Possible user requirements include address, route, and traffic separation; protection against intrusion, denial of service, and spoofing; confidentiality; CE authentication; data integrity; and protection against replay. The RFC does not say that every PPVPN must meet every listed requirement. Confidentiality, integrity, and anti-replay apply in this comparison only when the comparable private network also provided them.

Provider requirements may include authenticating control-plane sessions, limiting access to infrastructure devices, limiting the number of routes a customer can advertise, and controlling resource use on access links. The document also notes that configuration and operational processes matter because misconfiguration can breach isolation.
sections.plainLanguage: Customers may require their VPN traffic and routes to stay separate and may ask for secrecy, integrity, and authentication. The RFC lists possible requirements but does not make every item mandatory for every PPVPN.

sections.title: The Security Evaluation Template
sections.content:
The RFC provides a template for authors to evaluate a particular PPVPN approach. For each security assertion, the author records whether it is not applicable, fully or partly addressed by the base approach or an optional extension, handled outside the approach, or not met.

The template asks about address and route separation, improper cross-connections, confidentiality, authentication, integrity, replay protection, and control-protocol security. It also asks about denial-of-service protection, unstable or malicious customer networks, and vulnerabilities specific to the approach.
sections.plainLanguage: The template asks a technology author to report which security properties the design provides and which it does not. This lets readers compare technologies using the same questions.
